editorials.title: The number 10 shirt must not retire with Messi
editorials.passage:
When Lionel Messi announced his retirement from the Argentina national team last Monday, the reaction bordered on national mourning. Children cried in schools, journalists shed tears on television, newspapers filled their pages with emotional tributes and a telephone line was even opened for fans to express their gratitude to their idol. All weekend matches in Argentina were briefly stopped in the tenth minute as a tribute to the idol.

“I emptied myself. I have nothing more to give,” Messi wrote in his farewell.

It was an extraordinary end to an extraordinary relationship. For more than two decades, Messi had carried the expectations of a country that could never quite decide what it wanted him to be. He was compared endlessly with Diego Maradona, criticised for not displaying the same kind of passion and, for years, accused of somehow being less Argentinian because he had left for Barcelona as a child.

Yet by the time he walked away, the relationship between Messi and Argentina had been transformed. The player once treated as an outsider had become a national symbol in his own right.

“And we are full,” Jorge Valdano, a World Cup winner with Argentina in 1986, replied to Messi’s farewell. Messi may have emptied himself, but Argentina was full of everything he had given it.

Messi played 207 official matches over 21 years with his national team, an entire lifetime. He scored 125 goals and provided 68 assists. With him on the pitch, Argentina began every match with almost a goal guaranteed. He played in six World Cups, won one in Qatar in 2022, and reached two other finals. The last came less than two months ago in the United States, where, at 39 years old, he had his most productive World Cup, scoring eight goals and providing four assists.

His last great display came in the semifinal against England in Atlanta. Argentina trailed until the final minutes before staging a spectacular comeback to win 2-1, one of the most celebrated victories in the history of the national team.

For Argentina, beating England has never been just about football. The rivalry is inseparable from the dispute over the Malvinas Islands and the 1982 war. After the semifinal, the players unfurled a defiant anti-colonialist banner asserting Argentina’s claim. Beating England means beating the old Empire. And for Argentinian football, it inevitably evokes another number 10: Maradona, whose defining 1986 World Cup included that other historic victory over England.

Messi’s own victory over England would prove to be his last great display. Four days later, there was little left. Exhausted, he was barely involved as Spain dominated the final but needed extra time to win 1-0. “My legs gave out on me,” he later wrote in a public letter to his father, who died 20 days after the match.

Much of the international press accused Messi and Argentina of “not knowing how to lose”. As Spain received the World Cup a few metres (feet) away, the Argentinian players remained on the pitch with their backs turned towards the ceremony, after a few of them had been involved in a brief but ugly confrontation following the match.

The scene was not pleasant. But look at it through Messi’s eyes, and it becomes something else. He stood still, tears in his eyes, looking towards the supporters who loved him. What others saw as gracelessness in defeat was also a farewell. Messi already knew that this was goodbye. And, for the first time, his dying father could not be there with him.

Messi had once been criticised relentlessly in Argentina because, for all his success elsewhere, he spent more than a decade failing to win a major title with the national team. He even walked away from it once, in 2016, before coming back. Today, he leaves as a symbol of persistence, a rarity in times when everything is fleeting.

His departure has also prompted calls for Argentina to retire the number 10 shirt in his honour.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA), which published an emotional farewell video, will not do so. In official competitions, FIFA’s squad-numbering rules make that impossible. Argentina has been here before.

When Diego Maradona died in 2020, during the social isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic, the grief was overwhelming. “I would steal Maradona’s coffin and carry it through every neighbourhood of poor kids … until the sun, the rain, the earth and the wind turned it into ashes that would fly across the entire territory of the homeland,” the poet Liliana Campazzo wrote at the time.

There were calls then, too, to retire the number 10. But doing so would have taken the shirt away from Messi, who had worn it for Argentina since 2009 and was still writing his own history in it.

That matters because in Argentinian football, the number 10 has never been just a squad number. Traditionally worn by the great creative player, it became a distinction reserved for the true genius of the team. Maradona gave it eternal significance after Mexico 1986. Messi then made it his own.

Pele had already made the number 10 synonymous with footballing genius on the world stage, and generations of great players followed. But nowhere has the shirt carried quite the same weight as in Argentina, where it passed from Maradona to Messi.

Maradona and Messi played in 10 of the last 12 World Cups in which Argentina competed. Each won one: Maradona in 1986 and Messi in 2022. Between them came three more appearances in World Cup finals: Italy 1990 for Diego, Brazil 2014 and the United States in 2026 for Leo. Together, they scored 29 World Cup goals.

The numbers tell us how much Argentina owed them on the pitch. They do not explain what each came to mean beyond it. And the two men could hardly have been more different.

Diego was all excess, generosity and caprice. Millions of Argentinians became his “emotional slaves”, as the Spanish journalist Ramon Besa once wrote. Leo, by contrast, has always been far more reserved, perhaps because he witnessed Diego’s decline at close quarters and saw the price of fame.

Messi did not inherit Maradona’s number by becoming another Maradona. He carried the same enormous expectation in an entirely different way and, eventually, made the number his own. Whoever comes next will have to do the same.

These are days of mourning and orphanhood for the national team. Argentina has lost Maradona, and now, from the pitch at least, it has lost Messi. But Argentina has always been a factory of great players, and football lives on the hope that there can always be another.

In Spanish, we say “no hay dos sin tres”: “There is no two without three”. There is no third yet. Perhaps there never will be another Maradona or another Messi. But retiring the number 10 would mean giving up on the possibility.

Argentina is not ready to do that.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: ‘Laugh With Me’: Ruskin Bond offers poignant, humorous anecdotes about his writing career
editorials.passage:
The writerly life can look like one never-ending party to readers who track their favourite authors on social media, hopping from book signings to literature festivals to award ceremonies. But this seductive illusion conceals the messy and uncomfortable realities that many authors have to live with. Ruskin Bond’s new book, Laugh With Me, is a joy to read because it sheds all pretence.

A first-person narrative by Bond, who celebrated his 92nd birthday in May of 2026, it grants privileged access to the inner world of a celebrated writer, and makes one chuckle along. He writes, for instance, of a time in his late twenties when he felt that his publishers were not doing enough to publicise a newly published short story collection, as a result of which it was not available in bookstores at Khan Market, Connaught Place, and Shankar Market in Delhi.

His frantic search led him to Janpath, where he found a copy at a small bookshop. “It was firmly wedged at the bottom of a pile of other writers’ bestsellers – Khushwant Singh, Shobha Dé, Harold Robbins, Vikram Seth, Roald Dahl – everyone on top of poor little RB,” he writes. This anecdote will strike a chord with every debut author, wallowing in self-pity, and wondering if their book would have stood a better chance at being discovered if it were endorsed by a celebrity, represented by a star literary agent, or launched at an exclusive club with canapés and cocktails.

Bond’s candid recollection of how “desperate” he was as a young writer is all the more poignant because he has now become so popular that other authors are envious of him. The grouse that his books, along with Sudha Murty’s, hog shelf space at the expense of others writing for children is routinely heard when writers gather at literature festivals in India. It is humbling to know that Bond, too, has struggled to build a loyal readership.

In Laugh With Me , Bond goes on to spill embarrassing details about how he dealt with jealousy. When he thought that the Janpath bookshop owner wasn’t looking, he pulled out his book from the bottom of the pile and placed it at the top to make customers notice. “But the shop owner had seen me at my shameless attempt to display my neglected masterpiece,” recalls Bond.

Not knowing that the author of the book was standing before him, the owner said, “Ye nahin chalta!” (No one buys this one). The book was put back in its place, just like Bond. The author, however, was unstoppable in his zeal, so he revealed his identity. To his utter surprise, the man said, “I thought so. Writers are my best customers. They are always buying their own books.”

This part of Laugh With Me is a powerful commentary on the broken publishing ecosystem in India that pushes authors to champion their own books online and on offline platforms, which takes away from the time that could be spent writing their next book. This is simultaneously a tender portrait of the burning desire to be read, which leads many to write in the first place.

Bond turns self-deprecating humour into a survival strategy. “Writers are a vain lot. Everyone thinks he’s another Shakespeare or Kalidas, and that their books are going to be bestsellers,” he remarks, adding, “Well, Shakespeare did not make much money from writing, and I doubt if Kalidas went in for mass marketing, so we shouldn’t expect too much from our literary efforts.”

This line of thought might not go down well with authors who feel that they earn peanuts in terms of advances and royalties, while their creative labour pays the salaries of publishers, editors, designers and marketing professionals. Some of them spend out of their own pocket to hire publicists.

In the absence of financial security, authors often find comfort in fellowship and community. Bond, for example, writes about friends who gathered to celebrate the publication of his first story in a national newspaper when he was 16 years old. The cheque he got was for Rs 50. “That may not seem much today, but 75 years ago, it was a fair amount – almost the same as getting Rs 5000 for a story today,” he notes. He bought jalebis, samosas, pakoras, laddoos, pastries and lemonade. The party was thrown on the roof of the building where he lived.

Guess who decided to gatecrash this party? A group of monkeys! “Samosas were flying around, pastries were on the ground, jalebis were being fought over…and laddoos were bouncing around like pong-pong balls,” he recalls. Since nothing was left for humans to consume, they pooled in their contributions and went out to gorge on chaat, tikkees, golgappas and buttermilk.

This is a heartwarming tale in itself but Bond’s entrepreneurial mindset is the unexpected hero. “I made good use of my failed party by writing and selling a story about it, so in the end I had the last laugh.” This is the kind of jugaad that writers often have to resort to, where every disaster and disappointment becomes material to be mined for a future story, poem, novel or essay.

Perhaps the funniest part of Laugh With Me is where Bond confesses that he has been mistaken for other writers. What could have been a severe blow to his ego becomes an opportunity to giggle at the sheer absurdity of life. Once, a woman brought along her son of seven or eight and said, “Vicki wants your autograph; he’s reading one of your books in class.” Vicki was reading The Adventures of Tom Sawyer . Bond did not want to let him down, so he signed as Mark Twain.

On another occasion, Bond was approached at an airport by a lady who mistook him for Rudyard Kipling. She asked him when he was going to write another Mowgli story. He did not correct her or get angry. He simply told her that it was coming along nicely. The book documents another incident at a five-star hotel where a drunk lady said, “So you’re that writer fellow Buskin Ronde, aren’t you?” This is hilarious to read, especially as a journalist who covers literature festivals and often runs into authors who are horrified when an influencer who has just taken a selfie with them turns around and says, “Sorry, what’s your name? I would like to tag you on Instagram.”

Having lived through ups and downs for more than nine decades, Bond has learned to loosen up and not take things too seriously. “I take all this in good humour. Just as long as my royalty cheque gets my name right.” These little jibes, scattered throughout the book, are hugely entertaining. Bond reminds us that “anger and resentment poison the soul”, so a gentle disposition and the ability to “laugh at yourself from time to time” are the key to happiness.

Shamika Chaves’s whimsical design and illustrations elevate the book from an autobiographical work to an art object. She plays with typography, white space, and colour palettes, encouraging readers to pause and relish instead of rushing to read from cover to cover. This approach complements Bond’s writing style, which is languorous, dreamy and soaked in nostalgia.

Chintan Girish Modi has contributed to various anthologies, including 101 Indian Children’s Books We Love (2013), Borderlines: Volume 1 (2015), Clear Hold Build (2019), Fearless Love (2019), and Bent Book (2020). He can be found @chintanwriting on Instagram and X.

Laugh With Me , Ruskin Bond, designed and illustrated by Shamika Chaves, HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: Maafi, Kafi, Anchahi: The unwanted daughters in Haryana’s voter rolls
editorials.passage:
The names of some women voters stood out while I was looking up my parents’ details in the 2002 voter list for the Special Intensive Revision exercise being conducted in Haryana.

“Bhateri” and “Bharpai” seemed to be common names that were repeated across voter lists. Bhateri comes from the Haryanvi word “bhatera”, which means enough, while the word “Bharpai” indicates something that is surplus or plentiful.

It was an unsettling realisation that these names for women were common up until a few decades ago.

They are a reflection of Haryana’s deep-seated preference for sons. The 1981 Census noted that Haryana had only 870 females per 1,000 males, far below the national average of 933 females per 1,000 males. Voters born around 1981 would have been at least 21 years old when the SIR was conducted in 2002.

Conversations with women in my family and neighbourhood revealed that these names were quite common in Haryana till some decades ago. For the women bearing such names, it was humiliating but also something they had come to live with.

I asked my neighbour, also named Bhateri, what she felt about her name. She sighed and said, “Bebe, bhunda to lagya ae kare.” Sister, it does feel deeply unpleasant.

She added: “It is humiliating to be labelled as a burden to your family.”

An aunt recalled how in her village, Dubaldhan Majra, a neighbour’s daughter-in-law had seven daughters, the youngest named “Khatam”, which means finish or stop. The woman’s eighth child was a son.

The older women I spoke to expressed little distress about such names, saying that it was common, and some even believed that such names were effective in stopping more daughters from being born in a family.

Younger women with such names, though fewer in numbers, were more indignant and critical. A 36 -year-old woman named Maafi, which means forgiveness, recalled that when she moved to Rohtak for higher education, her name evoked surprise, discomfort and even ridicule from her classmates.

When Maafi would introduce herself, she would be asked, “Ayein, kitni bhaan ho tham? Tu aakhri hai ke?” How many sisters are you in total? Are you the last one?

Maafi said names like hers were humiliating but also conveyed how her family viewed women and gender rights. She said her name was also an indicator of her family’s social and economic background as one with limited access to education and not very well-off.

Maafi considered getting her name officially changed, but the long-drawn out, legal-bureaucratic process dissuaded her. Although she is known as Maafi in her natal village, she introduced herself as “Tamanna” in her marital village, a name she has informally taken on. She asserts that it is a step towards changing how the world sees her.

The history of such disparaging names likely stretches back to the 1940s and 1950s. According to my broad estimate, some of the women with such names in the electoral lists for my neighborhood were in their late 60s and early 90s.

Conversations with women in my neighbourhood uncovered more unpleasant names. Older and even younger women as they remembered the names of their friends, aunts, neighbours, relatives and grandmothers.

Some of these names included Dadka, which in Haryanvi refers to the sound produced when something burdensome falls unexpectedly from above; Dhapa, comes from Dhap in Haryanvi, which refers to a state of being “full”, here, referring to the number of girls in a family; Rambhateri literally translates to a request to God that “we have had enough girl children”.

Bohti, is a translation of the Hindi word “bohot”, which means more than enough; Sarli, which refers to something being suitably enough; Baadho, comes from the Haryanvi word for extra; similarly themed names were Anchahi, or unwanted, and Manbhari, which means no more is required.

In the 1970s, advances in prenatal diagnostics came to India as well. Women I spoke to pointed out that usually, it was not the first or the second daughters who were given disparaging names but the fourth or the fifth daughter.

After the introduction of sex determination technologies, the possibility of having five or more daughters in a family reduced significantly. Women I spoke to believe this led to a decrease in the number of girls with such names, which suggests that this decline in the later decade was prompted by the misuse of sex determination technology and not necessarily due to a progressive change in the outlook of Haryanvi society.

In the later years, around the 1970s, women I spoke to said that popular names included Seema, the Hindi word for limit; Mafi, which suggested forgiveness from continuous female births; Kafi, or enough; Antima, which means last; Khamosh, or quiet, and Santosh, which means satisfied. These names reflect a remodelling of disparaging names where the prejudice was wrapped in an indirect and softer vocabulary.

Another set of names that caught my attention in the 2002 voter list were of women named after fruits and other edible items. Some of these names included Santro, derived from the Hindi word santra for the fruit orange; Angoori, from the word angoor, which in Hindi refers to grapes; Kelo/Kelapati from the Hindi word kela for banana; Anaro, from the Hindi word anar for pomegranate; Pataso, from the Hindi word patasa, which is a kind of sugar candy, and Barfi, the milk-based sweet.

These names were not openly disparaging but nonetheless indicated a careless or even patronising attitude towards girl children, reducing them to objects of consumption.

The men’s names starkly differed: Mahaveer, or great warrior; Balwan, referring to one who is strong and well-built; Paramjeet, who is supreme in victory; Kuldeep, the light of the family; and the like. These names indicate the fondness with which sons were welcomed in the family, and the potential they were expected to achieve in their lives.

The names in Haryana’s 2002 voter rolls seem to reflect gendered prejudice from a previous era. But the state’s sex ratio in recent years indicates that Haryanvi society still favours male children.

Haryana’s sex ratio at birth showed signs of improvement, rising from 879 in 2011 to 923 by 2019. But it had plummeted to 895 girls per 1,000 boys in the first half of 2026.

Names constitute one’s identity but they are also repositories of the social values and cultural histories of communities we belong to. The names marking out the undesirability of women forced them to carry the weight of the perceived insignificance for their lifetime.

Though no longer pervasive anymore, these names are remnants of the state’s legacy of gender bias which persists in different forms, with different names.

Samiksha is a PhD student at the Centre for English Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University.

editorials.title: ‘China wants to be No. 1, India stands in its way’: Ex-diplomat on Beijing, BRICS and America
editorials.passage:
In an exclusive interview, Rajiv Dogra, former Ambassador to Italy, Romania, Moldova and Albania, and the last Indian Consul General in Karachi, Pakistan, discusses the forces that make nations rise and decline, the weakening of the US-led world order, and the wars in Ukraine and West Asia. In conversation with Firstpost, Dogra, who has just written a book, How Nations Fail and the Unmaking of America’s World, also discusses China’s ambitions, BRICS and the strategic choices confronting India.

The following is the first part of edited excerpts from the interview:

Q: In your new book, How Nations Fail, you examine democracies and authoritarian regimes. You say democracies are resilient in the long term but also have their own weaknesses. Can you explain what you mean?

A: Democracy is essentially a chicken-and-egg issue. You hold elections and, for four or five years, depending on the term, a certain set of people at the top carries out the mandate given to them. But the issue does not end there. Democracy must be constantly sustained. There has to be a bridge of trust between the leadership and the people, and there has to be constant dialogue. When that dialogue breaks down, when the leadership trusts only the people around it, democracy is in danger because the feedback system gets fractured. That is why democracy has to be more than just a game.

For example, today, can you call America a democracy? What is the difference between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping? Democracy is not just a label. Nor can democracy function amid anarchy. If there is anarchy, it becomes a non-functional democracy. If you look at Western Europe today, with a few exceptions, there has hardly been a leader whom you could call a real leader in the classical sense. Can such a country be called a functional democracy, or is it some form of unruly democracy? Trump is one example of the kind of political disruption that can weaken democratic institutions. Many European countries face a different form of democratic dysfunction. Democracy, in its true spirit, requires constant dialogue between the people and the leadership.

 HOW NATIONS FAIL AND THE UNMAKING OF AMERICA’S WORLD, by Rajiv Dogra

Q: Since you have written about Trump, I see a connection between that and the subheading of your latest book, ‘The Making of America’s World’. What makes you believe that America’s world order is now weakening?

A: In 1945, the world was recovering from the shock of the Second World War. America led; there was no doubt about it. An infrastructure emerged that was unparalleled in history. There was the World Bank, the IMF, the UN and a whole range of institutions. For Europe, there was the Marshall Plan. For the first time, there was a set of disciplines that, by and large, countries followed from 1945 onwards. America was leading that system by example. There were exceptions, of course, including the Vietnam War, but, broadly speaking, the world was moving towards greater prosperity. Even the two superpowers, America and the Soviet Union, balanced each other. The poor were becoming less poor and the rich were becoming richer. At least things were getting better.

What happened afterwards was that America developed an inflated ego. Beginning in the early 1960s, the term “Ugly American” came into use because Americans were increasingly seen as arrogant and as believing they could buy out everyone. The US sought to impose a form of neo-colonialism by grabbing resources around the world or changing governments and putting dictators in power. That was the first crack in the world order.

Then, after the Soviet Union collapsed, America became the sole superpower. It believed it could impose capitalism and its preferred political model across the world. But impositions do not always work. At the same time, America made the big mistake of helping China rise. China rose, but it was biding its time. Now it believes its time has come.

America did not continue to uphold the world order it had created. Under Trump, that order has been increasingly undermined. International institutions, including UN agencies, have been weakened. The only law Trump appears to recognise is his own interest. His actions concerning Iran, Russia and other countries represent a direct challenge to the existing order. It is not just Russia and Iran that are affected. Other countries, including India, are also affected by sanctions and by disruptions to energy and commodity markets. In a way, we are being sanctioned indirectly. The world order is being punctured almost daily. The consequences include increasing distrust and disruptions to supply chains. But does that mean the world order has broken down and that there will be a new world order tomorrow? I don’t think so.

World orders are not created overnight. They require planning and resources. America in 1945 accounted for roughly half of the world’s GDP. Today, no country has the same capacity. Moreover, America had a leadership role that China does not have at the moment. China is not interested in spending an extra yuan for the benefit of other countries. So, if you say there will be a new world order tomorrow, I think that is hoping for too much, too soon. Expectations need to be tempered.

 

Q: The Ukraine war has enormous economic and strategic consequences. How do you see it?

A: First, the misadventure in Ukraine was encouraged by Joe Biden. Some of his statements were interpreted as an open invitation to invasion. Having said that, this does not excuse Russia or Putin’s misadventure. Putin also underestimated the scale of the conflict. Marching into a country is one thing; holding it is entirely different.

European leaders should realise that the Russia-Ukraine war is not merely a Russia-Ukraine war. It affects every household in Europe, just as instability around the Strait of Hormuz affects households across Asia. War today has unfortunately become a matter of concern even for people who are not directly involved. Some European leaders thought that by supplying Ukraine with arms, they could take on Russia without the consequences reaching France, the UK or Germany. In Europe, fear of Russia has always existed, but it is misplaced. Russia is the country that has repeatedly helped defeat threats to Europe. Whether it was Napoleon or Hitler, Russia played a decisive role in their defeat.

Europeans made another mistake. For a long time, they talked about a European defence policy, but beyond the words, they did not put it into action. The situation is turning grimmer by the day. Even the much-tabooed N-word is being invoked these days. I think never since 1945 has the nuclear issue been discussed so loosely. Pakistan has repeatedly used nuclear threats since acquiring the bomb, but major powers have generally been more cautious about the nuclear question. The number of threats and references to nuclear escalation in the last year or so has been alarming. The world, and especially its leadership, needs to put a brake on this way of handling an issue as serious and potentially catastrophic as nuclear war.

 

Q: First Ukraine and now Iran — America seems to be on a mess-making spree. Iran, despite being in a severe economic crisis, has been giving the Americans a run for their money. What makes Iran different from a country such as Venezuela, and how do you see the Iran conflict developing?

A: Again, it is a case of national will. In Iran’s case, America made a huge mistake in assuming that the Iranian people were completely disconnected from their leadership. Perhaps there was dissatisfaction, but there was also nationalism. America’s misadventure resulted in nationalism becoming the dominant identity of Iran and the Iranian people. The second factor is, again, the lesson of history. America has not fully recovered from the Vietnam War. Look at Vietnam. A small country made America bite the dust, and afterwards it became one of Asia’s tiger economies. Iran, too, has shown that national will can prevail. The Iranian people have suffered enormously economically, but once the war is over, I have no doubt that sanctions will eventually ease and Iran will become another rising economy.

 

Q: India, too, has been in the American line of fire, especially since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. There are two views in foreign policy circles. One is that if Trump goes, things may return to normal. The other is that the damage has already been done, that America may not give India the support it needs, and that India may no longer trust America in the way it once did. What is your take?

A: First, India has never been one of America’s favourite children, and it never will be. We are mainly people-friendly, but we are not strategically aligned. America tends to push the world towards a very aggressive posture, whereas India is psychologically not made that way. The second thing is that India is too strong for someone to simply impose their will on it. Today, India wants to carve out its own space in the world. America has an entirely different view. There is not much space for independence. Trump or no Trump is not going to make any major difference to India-US relations.

On the other hand, India will have to consider the shape of the changing world. In the last year, so many new developments have taken place. The world may no longer be the same for India in the near future. In fact, that near future may be very near. In that eventuality, India cannot hope for much relief or much help from America. That raises the question of what India’s options are. And the options are limited.

 

Q: So, the impression I get from you is that this is not a very comforting time for India. At a time when America is playing difficult, how should India deal with China?

A: In my book War Time, while examining various scenarios, including the possibility of a Third World War, I found that the greatest chance of a world war beginning lay in a conflict between India and China. If that assumption is correct, then we have reason for caution. We have issues, whether they are admitted or not. The fact is that China does not really think India is succeeding. China’s ambition is quite clear: it wants to be number one in the world, replacing America. Whether it succeeds is a different matter. But that is its ambition.

And to proceed along that path, it first has to subjugate India. If these assumptions are correct, then we will always have an uneasy relationship with China. Sometimes even a small spark can lead to major problems, if not outright war. It would not be wise to rule out the possibility of frictions developing into something nastier.

 

Q: Taiwan is also high on China’s agenda. What is your take?

A: After Ukraine and Iran, any wise leader in the world would think twice before venturing into war and would consider what effect it would have on the country’s prestige and on the morale of its people. As far as China and Taiwan are concerned, if China sends landing ships, Taiwan has enough missile power to inflict significant damage and cause heavy loss of life among invading forces. Once Chinese forces land in Taiwan, there will also be resistance because Taiwan is preparing for it. Whether America comes in or not, whether Japan comes in or not, is a different issue. The fact is that it is not going to be a walkover. It will not be easy for Chinese forces. But we do not always have leaders who make entirely rational decisions.

 

Q: So, you believe the Ukrainian experience has restrained China from attacking Taiwan. Is that the case?

A: The Ukraine war has changed the picture because Chinese defence experts are monitoring every move. They are embedded there, and there is close coordination between the Russian and Chinese armies. But for the Ukraine war, China might not have hesitated to attack Taiwan. Please remember that when Margaret Thatcher met Deng Xiaoping and warned him against taking over Hong Kong, he reportedly said, “I’ll take it over in one afternoon.” That is not the case any more. China knows that it is far more powerful than Taiwan, but it also knows that it has to cross a sea.

 

Q: Especially when the economy is not doing too well. All is not well with China, given the number of PLA generals being purged and the problems facing the Chinese economy.

A: The problem for the world is that China is such a closed society that we do not know exactly what is happening. Often, speculation turns into theories that may not be correct. But definitely, all is not well. One clue is the number of generals Xi has dismissed. It has never happened before in China to this extent. That shows a sense of insecurity, which has not been commented upon very much. If they have all been dismissed for corruption, that also suggests there is something wrong with the system.

Another issue is unemployment in China. It is not as if new industries are coming up at the required pace. The housing sector has also acquired a bad reputation. America is a $38-39 trillion economy. China remains at around $20 trillion. If its economic crisis does not prove temporary, China may have to abandon its dream of becoming the No. 1 power.

China has, of course, made immense progress in defence and surveillance technology. But, once again, that does not make China No. 1 in the world. It makes China a major threat to the world, but not the supreme power.

 

Q: How do you see BRICS?

A: During the Cold War, we had the Non-Aligned Movement. People thought it was a paper tiger. There was nothing concrete about it. It did not have tanks or fighter aircraft. It was simply a collection of nations that met at the summit level and issued declarations. But the moral effect of non-alignment was huge. It was a stabilising force in a divided world.

BRICS is operating in a different environment. It is not really a collection of new poles of the world because “new poles of the world” is a much-misinterpreted term. No one is yet ready to become a pole.

 

Q: Except America and China?

A: Yes. But BRICS represents an alternative in terms of aspirations. These are the aspirations of countries that have either reached a position of growing influence, are close to it, or are moving towards it in one way or another. BRICS also has some achievements to its credit. At least it meets regularly at the summit level, and no major differences have so far derailed it.

The second thing is that it suggests an alternative. For example, replacing the dollar immediately is not realistic. But BRICS is at least thinking in terms of using national currencies and dealing with each other directly. So, there are definitely positives. When leaders meet, they do not discuss just rupees and yuan. They also discuss the state of the world. That carries a message beyond the summit rooms because the world is watching.

 

Q: Do you think India could have handled Trump differently?

A: One comment often heard is that we snubbed Trump in the run-up to the presidential elections. Trump is the kind of person who takes these things personally. But one cannot fault the Indian leadership for taking a cautious path then. So, theoretically, one could say that India could have handled Trump differently. But in practical terms, there is no denying that he is a changed man. He is not the Trump of his first term. He does not see reason in the same way.

(Part 1 for two-part interview)

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of former diplomat Rajiv Dogra. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Game of thrones: BRICS chairship will require extraordinary diplomatic dexterity from India
editorials.passage:
Just as India is getting ready to host the 18th BRICS annual summit from September 12, Chinese President Xi Jinping has been on a quiet but consequential visit to Egypt, a newly inducted member of BRICS that serves as a crucial geographical and political bridge linking the Arab world, Africa, and the Mediterranean.

Right off the SCO Summit in Bishkek, Central Asia, where China is aggressively shifting its footprint from extractive industries and resource imports through transnational pipelines towards digital infrastructure and renewable energy, Xi’s Egypt visit was an astute, tactical move.

His key economic objectives included currency swaps to bypass the US dollar and Western financial systems, advancing China’s digital footprint through major data and AI centres, expanding economic partnerships, and making Egypt a conduit for protecting Chinese interests in West Asia and Africa. Xi’s strategic manoeuvre is aimed at integrating a pivotal West Asian power deeper into China’s vision of an alternative global architecture, utilising technological infrastructure, de-dollarisation mechanisms, and expanding military cooperation to chip away at Western dominance in the region.

It is in this context that India is chairing the BRICS Summit. For all of India’s ambition and efforts at leading the Global South — an agenda it seeks to reinforce through minilateral frameworks such as BRICS — New Delhi neither has Beijing’s resources nor its ability to transform the grouping into a “Chinese bandwagon” through the weaponisation of economic interdependence.

And yet India can ill afford to let China walk away with the platform to further its own geopolitical objectives. For instance, turning it into a tool to influence emerging economies in Beijing’s strategic competition with the United States.

It helps explain why India, as the BRICS chair, has kept the focus firmly on the developmental agenda, guided by the theme: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, reflecting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of a “people-centric approach rooted in the spirit of Humanity First.”

New Delhi’s primary objective in BRICS is to act as a bridging power — a stabilising force that connects the developed world with the aspirations of the Global South. India, therefore, must steer the BRICS agenda towards substantive, constructive goals such as development finance, digital innovation, reform of global governance, counterterrorism and economic resilience. While acting as the voice of the Global South, India would look to prevent the grouping from falling prey to an overarching ‘anti-Western’ agenda.

And that cannot be done from the outside, looking in. On the never-ending questions around India’s participation in non-Western frameworks such as SCO or BRICS, the issue that is frequently overlooked is the unforgiving reality of geography and the imperatives of restoring the balance of power.

The war in Ukraine has accelerated the convergence of Moscow and Beijing. The tightening Sino-Russian embrace presents a strategic vulnerability for New Delhi. A Chinese monopoly over the Eurasian landmass may squeeze India’s traditional defence relationships and restrict New Delhi’s strategic space in Central Asia.

India cannot moderate or prevent this collusion from the outside. Whether or not frameworks such as SCO or BRICS serve India’s interests, ceding the non-Western institutional space to Beijing and allowing the Eurasian architecture to be designed at India’s direct expense is an act of stupidity. By maintaining a presence within these groupings, India inserts itself as a variable.

Moreover, overlapping frameworks such as BRICS provide middle powers with the tactical space to manoeuvre and engage multiple power centres without becoming tethered to any. India has proven adept at multidirectional diplomacy. Since the 2005 civil nuclear agreement with the US, New Delhi has systematically deepened its security, defence, technological, and intelligence integration with Washington. Yet, this deepening alignment has not come at the cost of India’s comfort in operating within non-Western spaces.

To quote from external affairs minister S Jaishankar’s book, The India Way, India aims to “engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, reassure Russia, bring Japan into play, draw neighbors in, extend the neighborhood, and expand traditional constituencies of support.”

The second, and perhaps more volatile, dynamic that India must manage is the fundamental tension that now defines groupings like BRICS: the clash between China’s hegemonic ambitions and India’s vision for a multipolar world.

Beijing interprets the traditional US-led international order as one in terminal decline. It wants to use vehicles like BRICS to challenge American primacy and install a China-centric model. Under the banner of ‘democratising’ international relations, Beijing has actively pushed to rapidly de-dollarise global trade, expand the bloc with nations that harbour anti-Western grievances, and weave its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) into the fabric of the Global South’s economy. In short, China is manoeuvring to position itself as the undisputed hegemon of the Global South.

This presents a challenge for New Delhi. India views China not merely as a systemic competitor but as a direct strategic rival occupying a contested geography, and both are locked in recurring military conflict along their shared Himalayan frontier.

The question, I think, worth exploring is how India, facing a permanent threat overhang from China, perceives its role in this period of profound geopolitical transition and how it may utilise the current geopolitical flux to its own advantage.

India’s strategy is rooted in the conviction that trading American unipolarity for a Chinese one is detrimental to the interests of the developing world. India envisions a true multipolar world — where it perceives itself as a pole — and a framework where power is reasonably distributed. Consequently, New Delhi uses the geopolitical transition to position itself as the credible, non-revisionist alternative to Chinese hegemony.

While Beijing offers the Global South opaque, debt-laden infrastructure projects with heavy conditionalities, India utilises BRICS to champion transparent and sustainable development finance. A prime example is the New Development Bank (NDB), which India seeks to empower as a tool for sovereign capacity building instead of clientelism. Alongside, through its BRICS chairship, India is focused on “strengthening early warning systems, supply and value chains, trade, finance, social security, resilient agriculture, alongside community-led solutions.”

While China exports state-monitored digital ecosystems, India is leveraging the BRICS platform to offer its pioneering Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI). By sharing open-source, interoperable frameworks like the India Stack, New Delhi provides emerging economies with a pathway to technological modernity that avoids Chinese digital authoritarianism.

To successfully execute this affirmative agenda, however, India must ensure that the expanded forum does not devolve into an arena for the projection of geopolitical rivalries. The critical challenge for New Delhi as the host of the 18th Summit is to actively avert the ‘SCO narrative’ from prevailing over the BRICS mandate.

The Bishkek Declaration, for instance, saw the 10-member bloc express ‘deep concern’ over the West Asian conflict and explicitly condemn the “military strikes on the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, without naming any country. It stated that these actions violate international law and the UN Charter. For India, a signatory to the declaration, direct finger-pointing at the US and Israel is diplomatically unfeasible.

As Sharang Shidore points out in Foreign Policy, internal squabbling has been a common feature at BRICS. At the May 2026 foreign ministers’ meeting, the platform failed to issue a joint statement. “Acrimonious exchanges between Iran and the UAE roiled the meeting of national security advisors which followed. Iran insisted that BRICS’s condemnations of terrorism — a staple since the grouping’s early years — also include what it called ‘state terrorism,’ a reference to Tehran’s perceptions of the US and Israel. Most other members were reluctant to go that far.”

It remains for India, therefore, to quarantine bilateral disputes and direct the bloc’s energy towards tangible deliverables. Shaping the governance architecture of a true multipolar world demands nothing less.

BRICS chairship will require extraordinary diplomatic dexterity and a display of astute statecraft from India. New Delhi should constructively engage Beijing on shared global challenges facing the Global South, align with Moscow on energy security and continental stability, and foster a people-centric approach while deepening indispensable partnerships with the West.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: India’s AI data centre ambition meets a talent bottleneck
editorials.passage:
India is building the physical infrastructure of its AI future at remarkable speed. The Economic Survey 2025-26 projects that the country’s data-centre capacity will rise from about 1.4 GW in the second quarter of 2025 to around 8 GW by 2030. The Survey also notes that India generates nearly 20 per cent of the world’s data but hosts only about 3 per cent of global data centres, underlining both the opportunity and the infrastructure gap. It identifies energy availability as one of the structural constraints India will have to address if it wants to become a global AI data-centre hub.

The physical build-out, however, is only half the equation. The people who must design, commission, operate, secure and maintain these facilities could become the less visible constraint. As well-funded global hyperscalers and Indian technology companies accelerate their investments in AI-ready infrastructure, the availability of specialised talent could become as important as the availability of land, power and capital.

A Deep and Widening Talent Gap in AI Operations

A March 2026 report by Quess Corp, an Indian workforce-solutions and business-services company, estimates that India’s data-centre and cloud-infrastructure ecosystem currently employs about 86,000-90,000 professionals across more than 50 providers. It puts the Supply Sufficiency Index (SSI) for AI operations talent — a measure of how well available talent meets industry demand — at 47, while estimating a 73 per cent shortage in core IT-operations roles such as infrastructure monitoring, incident response and network management.

That’s a concerning talent gap on the data-centre shop floor that should raise a red flag immediately. The report also expects AI workloads to account for nearly 30 per cent of data-centre capacity by 2026, increasing demand for specialised cloud, DevOps, security and compliance skills.

Advanced AI data centres are considerably more demanding than the conventional server rooms that supported enterprise computing. They specifically require high-density computing, liquid cooling and AIOps capabilities, among other requirements such as advanced networking, power and thermal management, and specialised hardware orchestration. Much of the terminology can sound more complicated than it is. High-density computing simply means putting far more computing power into a given physical space.

More computing produces more heat, which makes power delivery and cooling more difficult. Liquid cooling removes heat directly from high-performance chips using circulating liquid rather than relying entirely on air. AIOps, or artificial intelligence for IT operations, uses software to detect unusual behaviour, predict failures and automate parts of infrastructure management. It can reduce routine intervention, but it does not eliminate the need for skilled people who understand what the systems are doing and what to do when they fail.

Reskilling Imperative and the Risk of Strategic Dependence

The skills required are therefore both specialised and increasingly multidisciplinary. Engineers need to understand electrical systems, cooling, networking, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity and automation rather than just one of these domains. The challenge is not that India lacks engineers. It is that the number of engineers with this particular combination of capabilities is much smaller than the number of engineers graduating from conventional technology programmes.

As an immediate measure, reskilling experienced telecom, cloud, electrical, mechanical and IT professionals could be faster than waiting for universities to produce an entirely new generation of data-centre specialists. That should form the long-term academic strategy for building the talent pipeline. Vendor-led academies, short industry certifications and hands-on training on operational infrastructure can help bridge the gap. Universities and technical institutes should also work more closely with data-centre operators to design programmes around actual infrastructure rather than theoretical curricula alone.

There is a useful warning from another rapidly expanding Indian industry: aviation. India’s experience with pilot shortages in certain widely used aircraft categories shows how quickly specialised talent gaps can constrain operations and force reliance on external expertise when expensive infrastructure expands faster than the supply of trained professionals. Airlines pay top dollar for foreign talent, considerably weakening their economic and operational leverage.

Data-centre engineers are not airline pilots, and the economics are different. But the underlying lesson is similar: when an industry expands faster than the supply of people with scarce, experience-intensive skills, companies do not simply leave expensive assets idle forever. They compete harder for the people who can operate them. Salaries rise, experienced employees move between companies, retention becomes harder and organisations can become dependent on a small pool of specialists. Eventually, that competition can extend beyond India.

Without Skilled Operators, AI Infrastructure Risks Strategic Dependence

A country that builds massive AI infrastructure but does not build sufficient domestic expertise could find itself importing specialised talent to commission and operate parts of that infrastructure. That would not mean foreign expertise is undesirable. Global talent is an asset. The concern is strategic dependence: repeatedly paying a premium for scarce expertise that should have been developed domestically can weaken the economic advantage created by building the infrastructure in the first place.

The Economic Survey’s warning on energy adds another dimension. Data centres are highly energy- and resource-intensive, and AI workloads increase that intensity. The Survey explicitly identifies energy shortages as a structural constraint on India’s ambition to become a global AI data-centre hub. The implication is straightforward: a data centre requires far more than land, buildings and servers. It requires dependable power, cooling, networks, security and, ultimately, people who know how to keep all of those systems working together.

India should therefore expand its definition of data-centre infrastructure. A trained engineer, a certified operator and an experienced infrastructure manager are as much a part of the compute ecosystem as a power substation or a server rack.

The country has an enormous advantage: a large technology workforce, decades of experience in global IT operations and a deep pool of engineers who can be retrained. The talent problem is therefore solvable. But it will not be solved automatically by the market, because specialised expertise takes time to accumulate. The experience required to manage complex infrastructure cannot be created by issuing certificates alone.

India’s AI data-centre ambition is real, and the opportunity is too large to approach it pessimistically. But the sequencing matters. Building gigawatts of computing capacity first and asking later whether enough people know how to operate it risks putting the cart before the horse.

The aviation experience offers a warning of what happens when talent planning follows capacity expansion rather than anticipating it: scarce expertise becomes expensive, employee churn accelerates and dependence on external talent increases. India should not wait for its data-centre boom to reach the same point.

The country needs a war-footing approach to data-centre talent now. Not after the next gigawatt is commissioned. India’s AI infrastructure will ultimately be defined neither by the amount of capital invested nor by the number of megawatts installed. It will be defined by whether we have the people capable of turning that physical capacity into reliable, competitive and strategically valuable compute.

(Sreejith Sreedharan is a technology analyst and author of ‘Future of Work – AI Augmented Autonomous Decentralised’. He works on organisational AI readiness and created the AI Instinct Index®, a psychometric diagnostic designed to assess behavioural readiness for AI adoption and adaptive capacity in constraint-heavy environments. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The near-death of the single-handed backhand — and a Federer lament
editorials.passage:
Liquid emotion was overflowing on the night.

Stan Wawrinka — 41 years old — one last time on the Grand Slam stage. Tennis was losing more than a three-time major champion; what was also bidding goodbye was one of its most compelling visual spectacles. Wawrinka’s signature shot — that glorious single-handed backhand, released with such ferocity that the ball appeared to leave his racket offended — was now part of folklore.

The Wawrinka backhand was an event in itself, captured in slow-motion replays and poetic phrases by swooning writers over the years. He delivered it with the shoulder turned, the chest opened and his racquet sweeping through a magnificent arc. It was mesmeric and enraptured watchers in arenas and on TV. A rival once extolled that when hit down the line, the Wawrinka backhand felt like being struck by a bolt of lightning.

In sport, the sub-plots within grand battles are often about the execution of a sublime skill. Few strokes combine power and beauty as effortlessly as the single-handed backhand. There is a touch of defiance in the image it generates — an intricate, demanding stroke performed in a sport that has increasingly structured itself around the mantra of “efficiency” in the modern age.

For generations, the single-handed backhand was central to tennis’ visual language. Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall carried it through an earlier age. John McEnroe caressed the ball, Ivan Lendl drove through it and Stefan Edberg made it an essential component of his elegant forward movement to the net. Boris Becker blasted it with muscular disdain and Pete Sampras unfurled his version as an ally to a visceral running forehand and powerful serve.

There were others, of course, who captivated fans with its jaw-dropping beauty. Gustavo Kuerten, Richard Gasquet and Dominic Thiem among the men and Steffi Graf, Gabriela Sabatini and Justine Henin among the women demonstrated that one hand could create both astonishing angles and formidable power.

And then there was Roger Federer.

Federer’s version of the stroke, like much else in his game, contained multitudes. He could roll it crosscourt, knife a slice that kissed the surface and hissed like a snake or flick a passing shot from a seemingly impossible position. It complemented everything else about his play — lightness of movement, variety and the impression that he was discovering possibilities that simply did not occur to the mortals across the net.

Yet, in a detailed breakdown at a press event before the US Open began, Federer was asked to pontificate on the near disappearance of the stroke. He nodded along, with an almost sad smile on his face, when told by a reporter that no single-handed player had reached a Grand Slam semi-final in the first three majors of 2026.

The Swiss genius was eager to burrow down this rabbit hole. The decline, he reckons, begins long before players reach the professional circuit. Federer estimates that 90 per cent of his childhood coaches used one hand. Today, he says, coaches are predominantly two-handed players and “it’s easier to teach a kid” the same technique.

Modern tennis demands early results. The double-hander offers young players greater stability, especially when they lack the strength required to control the racquet with one arm. The single-hander takes longer to build, and Federer mused that patience can evaporate quickly.

“Everything has to happen immediately,” was his assessment.

Once consumed by the subject, Federer began pulling on different threads. He reflected on how training when he was a junior was divided almost equally between baseline play and movement towards the net. Now, he reckons, the balance is closer to 90-10 in favour of the baseline. Slower conditions, heavier exchanges, advanced strings and the ballast of the modern return have created an environment in which two hands are the logical choice. Both hands on the racquet allow players to absorb pace more easily, control high-bouncing balls and have options when caught out of position.

In sport, evolution is inevitable and this isn’t a lament for a better age — after all, players build themselves to win. Yet, romantics can’t help but ruefully sigh about the price efficiency has extracted. As Wawrinka left New York, it felt like tennis was saying goodbye not only to a champion but to a form of expression. Lorenzo Musetti, Stefanos Tsitsipas and a few others still keep it alive, but these players have become a very minor exception to a firmly established norm.

Federer remains “hopeful that it’s not the end” and beauty, after all, has a way of surviving even when cold logic wins the day. Yet, each time a single-handed backhand is now unfurled, it feels like a flourish from tennis’ past that is briefly illuminating its present. Precious and rare.

(Gaurav Kalra is an award-winning sports media executive, broadcaster and content strategist with over three decades of experience telling stories from the heart of Indian and global sport. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Explained: New Visa Limits Put Foreign Students at Risk in Trump's America
editorials.passage: The Trump administration is revising a visa rule for international students that in part determines how long, and under what conditions, they can stay in the country. The change sounds technical. Its effects are not.Beginning 15 September 2026, most students entering the US on F-1 and J-1 visas—meaning visas for international students and exchange visitors, including students and scholars—will no longer be admitted for “duration of status.” Duration of status means they can remain in the US as long they are enrolled in their academic program, or shortly thereafter.Now, academic visa holders will instead be able to stay in the country for a predetermined period of time, generally four years. Those who need more time to complete a degree will have to reapply to US Citizenship and Immigration Services for permission to stay.The change could also complicate international travel: Students returning to the US will have to make sure their fixed period of admission has not expired, in addition to having the valid visa and school documents normally required for reentry.The rule also lets full-time international students stay 30 days in the country after they complete their program, as opposed to the 60 days they currently have to remain in the USI study the history of international students in US higher education. Universities rely on international students for tuition, teaching, research and other kinds of skilled work.These new rules will make it harder for some international students to visit and stay in the country, a result that will likely have negative consequences for universities and colleges, too.US Pauses Visa Appointments Worldwide Amid Trump's Immigration CrackdownUS colleges and universities hosted 1,177,766 international students in the 2024-25 school year, an all-time high that made up approximately 6 percent of all higher education students.Most of them were working toward degrees in in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.Nearly 488,500 of those international students were seeking graduate degrees. More than 294,000 of them participated in a federal program called Optional Practical Training (OPT), which helps some international students work in jobs related to their field of study before or after they graduate.International enrollment grew steadily at US colleges and universities, from about 565,000 students in the 2004-05 school year to more than 1 million by the 2015-16 academic year.Growth then slowed during the first Trump administration but began rising again after 2021.The concentration is much higher in some programs and institutions. At Purdue, for example, international students make up 63 percent of graduate students in mechanical engineering. At Columbia University, non-US residents made up 53 percent of graduate students in the fall of 2024.Since 2024, the greatest number of international students has come from India. The next largest group is students from China. For more than a decade, students from China made up the largest group of international students in the US But the number of Chinese students has dropped over the past several years.International students are important for university finances, too. Most of these students are not eligible for US federal student aid or loans.More than half of international students report “personal or family funds” as their primary source of financial support to help pay for their education. These students contributed nearly US$55 billion to the US economy in 2024, according to the international student exchange nonprofit Institute of International Education.International graduate students also frequently teach undergraduate courses, conduct experiments and staff research laboratories.US to Suspend Immigrant Visa Processing For 75 Countries From 21 JanuaryUntil now, most international students did not have to reapply to maintain or extend their standard F-1 student visa midway through their course of study.And if a student remained enrolled and complied with immigration rules, a university could extend the student’s expected completion date of their program when more time was needed.The new rule introduces a separate federal immigration review for every student whose course of study goes beyond four years. This, according to the Department of Homeland Security, will add 393,500 new visa reviews to the US government workload each year.Academic work does not always proceed on schedule. Research changes direction. Funding gets delayed. A dissertation needs another semester.If a student reaches the end of their visa’s limits before they finish their degree, a university can still say that the student is making appropriate progress and needs more time—but now the US government will also have to agree that the student can remain enrolled and stay in the country.The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration is among the higher education groups that has warned the change could disrupt teaching and research, as well as discourage students from choosing a US school altogether.The Department of Homeland Security has acknowledged that the change may be disruptive. But the agency argues that fixed student visa time periods will give immigration officials more opportunities to check whether students are following visa requirements and to conduct national security screening.H-1B Lottery Discarded: How New US Visa Rules Will Impact Indian ProfessionalsThe first Trump administration proposed a similar policy in 2020. The Biden administration withdrew this visa proposal in 2021. Trump then revived the proposal after returning to office.This policy change comes alongside other immigration changes that make it harder for international students to attend US schools.In 2025, the Trump White House tried unsuccessfully to stop Harvard from enrolling any international students. Federal courts blocked that measure in June 2025.Secretary of State Marco Rubio also announced in May 2025 that the State Department was beginning to revoke visas of some Chinese students and increasing the scrutiny of prospective international students from China and Hong Kong.The administration said in January 2026 that it had revoked 8,000 student visas since the start of Trump’s second term.Trump Administration Suspends Green Card Lottery After Brown University ShootingThe new rule does not end international education or impose a four-year maximum on all students’ degrees. It does mean, however, that more international students will need to get additional levels of federal approval so they can complete their education in the US.A student in a six-year doctoral program can still finish their degree, but they will generally need federal approval to remain in the country beyond four years. A student in a two-year master’s program who finishes on schedule may never need an extension.The four-year limit can also affect students whose programs are designed to take longer. The University of Cincinnati’s engineering degree generally takes five years to complete, for example. Some medical residency and fellowship pathways for J-1 physicians routinely extend five to seven years.These new roadblocks can determine whether students finish degrees, or remain with their partners and children. They can also determine whether laboratories keep researchers and employers retain graduates trained in the USOn 18 August, a coalition of higher education groups and unions sued to block the rule, arguing that requiring students to repeatedly seek federal permission to continue their studies will disrupt degree programs and make it harder for universities to recruit and retain students.International students are woven into the everyday work of US higher education. Making their ability to stay more dependent on repeated federal decisions will inevitably affect the institutions that rely on them.(Abigail Boggs is an Assistant Professor of Sociology and Education Studies at Wesleyan University.
